mona.title: Mona Lisa
mona.author: Leonardo da Vinci
mona.background: Although Leonardo da Vinci painted Lisa, the wife of a Florentine silk merchant, he never handed the work over to the patron, keeping it with him even when he moved to France in his final years. His sfumato technique—layering dozens of ultra-thin glazes of oil paint—creates living light and atmosphere without a single hard outline.
mona.look: Start by gazing into her eyes. The moment your focus shifts to her mouth, doesn't her smile seem to vanish? Leonardo carefully calculated how human peripheral vision perceives blurred contours. Also notice the subtle trick in the background: the horizon sits at different heights on the left and right.

venus.title: Venus de Milo
venus.author: Ancient Greek Sculptor
venus.background: Carved in Hellenistic Greece around 130 BC, this statue was unearthed by chance in 1820 by a farmer digging behind a stone wall on the Aegean island of Melos. With its graceful S-curve twist and the drapery cascading from her hips, it is celebrated as a pinnacle of ancient sculptural beauty.
venus.look: Don't just view her straight on—step slightly to the side. Her shoulders and hips twist gently in opposite directions, creating a sense of poised tension as though she might move at any instant. Whether her lost arms once held an apple or a mirror, the space left to our imagination is part of the statue's enduring magic.

victory.title: Winged Victory of Samothrace
victory.author: Ancient Greek Sculptor
victory.background: Dedicated around 190 BC at the sanctuary on the northern Aegean island of Samothrace to thank the gods for a naval victory, this monument originally stood atop a rocky outcrop and water basin, depicting Nike, goddess of victory, alighting onto the prow of a warship.
victory.look: Looking up at the sculpture as you climb the grand staircase recreates the experience of the ancient sanctuary itself. Pay close attention to the wet drapery clinging to her body in the fierce sea wind and the fabric billowing dramatically behind her. Even without a head or arms, her entire form resonates with the energy of wind and forward motion.

liberty.title: Liberty Leading the People
liberty.author: Eugène Delacroix
liberty.background: Witnessing the fervor of the July Revolution of 1830—when Parisians rose up against tyranny—Delacroix completed this masterpiece in just three months. The central female figure is not a real person, but an allegory embodying the ideal of Liberty herself (Marianne).
liberty.look: The red cap on Liberty's head is a Phrygian cap, worn by freed slaves in ancient Rome as a badge of freedom. Look past the gunsmoke on the far right to spot the twin towers of Notre-Dame Cathedral, and take in the diverse crowd alongside her, from an intellectual in a top hat to a young street boy.

catalog-0001.title: The Coronation of Napoleon
catalog-0001.author: Jacques-Louis David
catalog-0001.background: Court painter Jacques-Louis David captured the December 1804 imperial coronation at Notre-Dame Cathedral on an overwhelming scale nearly ten meters wide. Rather than the moment Napoleon placed the crown on his own head, David chose the instant he crowns Empress Joséphine.
catalog-0001.look: Look for the woman seated prominently in the central box in the background. She is Napoleon's mother, Letizia—who actually boycotted the ceremony in protest and never attended. Prioritizing the emperor's idealized staging over historical fact is the most fascinating political sleight of hand in this painting.

catalog-0002.title: The Raft of the Medusa
catalog-0002.author: Théodore Géricault
catalog-0002.background: In 1816, the French frigate Méduse ran aground off the coast of Africa; when its incompetent aristocratic captain monopolized the lifeboats, 147 people were cast adrift on a makeshift raft. Only fifteen survived the thirteen-day ordeal. Twenty-seven-year-old Géricault took on this national scandal.
catalog-0002.look: Scan the horizon on the far right for a tiny speck no larger than a grain of rice—that is the rescue ship Argus. A sweeping triangular composition surges upward from despair and death in the lower left to figures frantically waving cloth at the upper right, conveying humanity's cry rising from the depths of hopelessness.

catalog-0003.title: The Wedding at Cana
catalog-0003.author: Paolo Veronese
catalog-0003.background: Hanging directly opposite the Mona Lisa, this is the largest painting in the Louvre. Painted in 1563 for the refectory of the Benedictine monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, it transformed the dining hall so the monks felt they shared every meal at Christ's table.
catalog-0003.look: The man dressed in white playing a stringed instrument at the center is Veronese himself, seated next to the master Titian in red. Notice the small hourglass on the musicians' table and the butcher carving meat directly above Christ's head—quiet foreshadowings of the Passion hidden within a sumptuous feast.

catalog-0004.title: Oath of the Horatii
catalog-0004.author: Jacques-Louis David
catalog-0004.background: Unveiled in 1784, just five years before the French Revolution, this Neoclassical manifesto took Europe by storm. Depicting three Roman brothers swearing to fight for their nation's fate, it proclaimed an uncompromising resolve to sacrifice personal affection for civic duty.
catalog-0004.look: Compare the shapes on the left and right sides of the canvas. The men on the left form sharp straight lines and triangles of iron will, while the women on the right collapse in soft, weeping curves. One of those sisters is engaged to an enemy warrior whom her brothers are about to face in battle.

catalog-0005.title: Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss
catalog-0005.author: Antonio Canova
catalog-0005.background: Italian Neoclassical master Antonio Canova carved the most romantic moment of love's awakening in Greek mythology out of pure white marble: Cupid, god of love, gently revives Princess Psyche with a kiss after she has fallen into an eternal sleep.
catalog-0005.look: Step closer and look right between their lips—they are still separated by just a few millimeters. By freezing the fleeting instant immediately before they touch, Canova fills the viewer with poignant anticipation. Also marvel at how thinly the marble has been carved to give Cupid's wings a translucent delicacy.

catalog-0006.title: Code of Hammurabi
catalog-0006.author: Ancient Babylonia
catalog-0006.background: Enacted around 1750 BC by King Hammurabi of Babylon, this is one of the world's oldest written legal codes. Roughly 282 laws are densely inscribed in cuneiform across a gleaming black basalt stele standing 2.25 meters tall.
catalog-0006.look: Examine the relief carving at the very top of the stele: Shamash, the god of sun and justice, sits enthroned while King Hammurabi stands before him in reverence. Far from encouraging cruelty, the famous rule of 'an eye for an eye' was actually a groundbreaking legal limit designed to forbid excessive revenge beyond the harm done.

scribe.title: The Seated Scribe
scribe.author: Ancient Egypt
scribe.background: Discovered in a tomb at Saqqara and dating back roughly 4,500 years to Egypt's Old Kingdom, this painted limestone statue honors a literate official. Those who could read and write belonged to an elite, highly respected circle of learned administrators.
scribe.look: The statue's most startling feature is its eyes. Inlaid with rock crystal, white magnesite, and copper eyelids, they appear uncannily alive—no matter the angle you approach from, this figure from forty-five centuries ago seems to lock eyes directly with you.

lacemaker.title: The Lacemaker
lacemaker.author: Johannes Vermeer
lacemaker.background: Measuring barely 24 by 21 centimeters, this is the smallest of Vermeer's paintings, yet it shines like a jewel. With extraordinary concentration and mastery of light, he elevated a quiet moment of 17th-century Dutch domestic life into timeless stillness.
lacemaker.look: Look at the red and white threads spilling from the cushion in the foreground. Vermeer deliberately painted them softly blurred, keeping sharp focus solely on the woman's fingertips and needle behind them. Long before photography existed, his astonishing eye already understood optical depth of field.

catalog-0007.title: Winged Human-Headed Bull (Lamassu)
catalog-0007.author: Ancient Assyria
catalog-0007.background: In the 8th century BC, these colossal protective spirits—known as lamassu—guarded the palace gates of Dur-Sharrukin, the new capital built by Assyrian King Sargon II. Carved from single blocks of stone over four meters tall, they embody royal wisdom, strength, and divine authority.
catalog-0007.look: Try counting the creature's legs. Viewed from the front, it stands firmly on two legs; walk around to the side, and it strides forward on four. By carving five legs in total, Assyrian sculptors devised an ingenious optical trick so the guardian appears complete from every angle of approach.

dying.title: Dying Slave
dying.author: Michelangelo
dying.background: Carved between 1513 and 1515 for the monumental tomb of Pope Julius II, this unfinished masterpiece reveals Michelangelo at his most poetic. Rather than writhing in agony, the figure exudes a languid, sensual calm, as if slipping free from earthly bonds into deep slumber.
dying.look: Notice the band of cloth crossing his chest and the roughly sketched silhouette of a monkey emerging from the stone at his feet. Seeing a human form awaken from rough-hewn marble lets us witness Michelangelo's core philosophy firsthand: liberating the living soul trapped inside the stone.

catalog-0008.title: Grande Odalisque
catalog-0008.author: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
catalog-0008.background: Commissioned in 1814 by Napoleon's sister Caroline Murat, Queen of Naples, Ingres's painting sparked fierce controversy when first exhibited. Treating an Eastern harem subject, he boldly departed from strict realism in pursuit of pure linear grace and sweeping curves.
catalog-0008.look: Take a close look at the length of her back. Anatomically speaking, her spine has roughly three extra vertebrae, and her right arm is impossibly elongated. Ingres sacrificed strict human proportions for a continuous, musical flow of curves across the canvas.

catalog-0009.title: Rebellious Slave
catalog-0009.author: Michelangelo
catalog-0009.background: Designed as a pendant to the Dying Slave for the tomb of Pope Julius II, this unfinished marble sculpture captures the exact opposite emotion. Rather than yielding to sleep, the figure twists violently against invisible fetters in a fierce struggle for life and freedom.
catalog-0009.look: Follow the bulging muscles of his shoulder and the defiant angle of his head turned skyward from both the front and side. The rough, uncarved mass of marble clinging to his body feels like a cage of gravity itself, heightening the raw intensity of his resistance.

catalog-0010.title: Portrait of Louis XIV
catalog-0010.author: Hyacinthe Rigaud
catalog-0010.background: When the Sun King Louis XIV was sixty-three, he commissioned this state portrait as a gift for his grandson, the King of Spain. So delighted was he with the result, however, that he kept it in France and had it hung in the throne room at Versailles.
catalog-0010.look: Notice the striking contrast between his weathered, majestic sixty-three-year-old face and the slender, ballet-posed legs of a young dancer below. Louis XIV was an accomplished court dancer, and those red-heeled shoes and shapely legs were proud emblems of royal vigor and youth.

catalog-0011.title: Great Sphinx of Tanis
catalog-0011.author: Ancient Egypt
catalog-0011.background: Unearthed at the ancient city of Tanis in northeastern Egypt, this is one of the largest granite sphinxes outside Egypt. Probably carved around 4,600 years ago during the Old Kingdom, it was reinscribed by successive pharaohs who claimed its timeless prestige as their own.
catalog-0011.look: Admire the ancient artisans' skill in polishing hard pink granite to such smoothness, and spot the royal hieroglyphs carved into the chest and base. Uniting a human head for royal intellect with a lion's body for sovereign power, this guardian watched over temple precincts for millennia.

catalog-0012.title: The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne
catalog-0012.author: Leonardo da Vinci
catalog-0012.background: One of three masterpieces Leonardo kept in his studio until the end of his life and carried with him to France, still unfinished. It depicts three generations together: the Virgin Mary sits on her mother Saint Anne's lap while reaching out to hold back the Christ Child as he plays with a lamb.
catalog-0012.look: Compare Mary's tender, wistful expression with the innocent energy of Jesus clutching the lamb's ears. The lamb symbolizes his future sacrifice on the cross; knowing her son's fate, Mary tries gently to restrain him while Anne looks on calmly—all woven into a harmonious pyramidal composition.

catalog-0013.title: Virgin of the Rocks
catalog-0013.author: Leonardo da Vinci
catalog-0013.background: Commissioned as an altarpiece in Milan in 1483, this is the earlier of Leonardo's two versions (the second hangs in London's National Gallery). Inside a shadowy grotto, the Virgin and Christ Child encounter the young Saint John the Baptist and an angel in a scene of quiet mystery.
catalog-0013.look: Focus on the angel on the right. Looking directly out at us, the angel points toward the infant Saint John on the left. Through that single gaze and gesture, Leonardo draws us across the threshold of the canvas and invites us into the sacred gathering inside the cave.

catalog-0014.title: Saint John the Baptist
catalog-0014.author: Leonardo da Vinci
catalog-0014.background: Widely regarded as Leonardo's final painting, this work traveled alongside the Mona Lisa to the court of French King Francis I. Emerging from velvety darkness, a softly illuminated young John smiles enigmatically while pointing heavenward.
catalog-0014.look: Gone is the austere ascetic of the desert; instead, we meet an androgynous beauty with a haunting, knowing smile. The gentle rounding of his shoulder and raised arm emerging from deep shadow marks the ultimate triumph of sfumato, while his upward finger heralds the coming Redeemer.

catalog-0015.title: The Death of Sardanapalus
catalog-0015.author: Eugène Delacroix
catalog-0015.background: Inspired by a play by Lord Byron, Delacroix stunned the 1827 Salon with this Romantic tour de force. Besieged by rebels, the legendary Assyrian king Sardanapalus refuses to yield his treasures to his enemies, ordering his horses, riches, and concubines slaughtered before his eyes.
catalog-0015.look: Follow the crimson bed slashing diagonally across the canvas up to the upper left, where the king watches the carnage with chilling detachment. Bucking white horses, spilled gold vessels, and writhing figures swirl in a deliberate defiance of classical order and perspective—an intoxicating vision of Romantic excess.

catalog-0016.title: The Turkish Bath
catalog-0016.author: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
catalog-0016.background: Completed at the astonishing age of eighty-two, this circular painting stands as Ingres's lifelong summation of form and sensuality. Originally rectangular, he reshaped it into a tondo so the viewer feels as though peering through a keyhole into an intimate Eastern bathhouse.
catalog-0016.look: Look at the woman seated with her back to us in the foreground, strumming a mandolin. She is a direct reprise of the figure Ingres painted fifty-four years earlier in his celebrated Valpinçon Bather. Around her, more than twenty nude figures echo one another in rippling curves within the round frame.

catalog-0017.title: Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione
catalog-0017.author: Raphael
catalog-0017.background: High Renaissance master Raphael painted this supreme portrait of his close friend Baldassare Castiglione—diplomat, scholar, and author of The Book of the Courtier. Without theatrical props, Raphael distilled his friend's quiet intellect and nobility through muted grays and blacks alone.
catalog-0017.look: Notice how Raphael achieves extraordinary warmth and dignity without a single drop of bright red or gold—only gray fur, a dark cap, and luminous skin tones. Both Rembrandt and Rubens later sketched copies of this work, cementing its status as an eternal benchmark of portraiture.

catalog-0018.title: La Belle Ferronnière
catalog-0018.author: Leonardo da Vinci
catalog-0018.background: Attributed to Leonardo da Vinci during his years at the Milanese court, this poised portrait of an aristocratic woman takes its nickname—'La Belle Ferronnière'—from the jeweled band resting across her forehead. The painting is currently on loan to the Louvre Abu Dhabi.
catalog-0018.look: Watch how her torso faces left while her head turns smoothly toward a three-quarter gaze, and notice the faint rosy glow reflected onto her cheek from her red gown. Leonardo's keen scientific observation caught even the subtle bounce of colored light onto human skin.

catalog-0019.title: Pierrot (Gilles)
catalog-0019.author: Antoine Watteau
catalog-0019.background: Painted shortly before Antoine Watteau's death at just thirty-six, this enigmatic work by the great poet of 18th-century Rococo sets a comic stage clown at life-size in the very center of the canvas—revealing the quiet solitude behind theatrical laughter.
catalog-0019.look: Look at his ill-fitting white costume—sleeves slightly too long, trousers a touch too short—and his arms hanging limply at his sides. Cut off from the lively troupe carousing below, his steady, wistful gaze seems to mirror the artist's own awareness of approaching mortality.

catalog-0020.title: The Embarkation for Cythera
catalog-0020.author: Antoine Watteau
catalog-0020.background: Submitted in 1717 as Watteau's reception piece for the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture, this landmark work invented a brand-new genre: the fête galante. Set on Cythera, island of Venus, it captures aristocratic lovers bathed in a dreamlike golden twilight.
catalog-0020.look: Art historians still debate whether these couples are preparing to embark for the island of love or reluctantly departing as the dream fades. Trace the pairs from right to left and watch their body language shift gradually from hesitant courtship to tender embrace.

catalog-0021.title: The Astronomer
catalog-0021.author: Johannes Vermeer
catalog-0021.background: Infused with Vermeer's fascination with science, The Astronomer forms a celebrated pair with The Geographer in Frankfurt. Many scholars believe the model may have been Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, the Delft pioneer of the microscope and Vermeer's neighbor.
catalog-0021.look: Notice that the scholar's fingertips rest gently not on a terrestrial globe, but on a celestial globe, while a framed painting hangs on the wall behind him: The Finding of Moses. In biblical tradition, Moses was praised as 'learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians'—a quiet tribute to the pursuit of knowledge.

catalog-0022.title: Death of the Virgin
catalog-0022.author: Caravaggio
catalog-0022.background: Painted for a church in Rome by Baroque revolutionary Caravaggio, this canvas was rejected by the clergy as overly earthly and irreverent. Yet Peter Paul Rubens immediately recognized its genius and urged his patron to buy it on the spot.
catalog-0022.look: Take in the vast crimson curtain plunging from the top of the frame and the Virgin Mary lying motionless with bare, swollen ankles. Stripping away angels and theatrical miracles, Caravaggio turns dramatic light and shadow onto the raw, human grief of disciples mourning someone they deeply loved.

catalog-0023.title: Venus of Arles
catalog-0023.author: Ancient Roman Sculptor (restored by François Girardon)
catalog-0023.background: Echoing the graceful style of the 4th-century BC Greek master Praxiteles, this marble sculpture dates to the late 1st century BC. Excavated in the 17th century from the ancient Roman theater in Arles and presented to Louis XIV, it is currently on loan to the Musée départemental Arles antique.
catalog-0023.look: When discovered, the statue was missing both arms; Louis XIV's court sculptor François Girardon restored them holding a mirror and an apple. Look closely at how ancient Greek bodily grace merges seamlessly with the refined restoration ideals of 17th-century France.

catalog-0024.title: Dendera Zodiac
catalog-0024.author: Ancient Egyptian Artisans
catalog-0024.background: Carved around 50 BC for a chapel ceiling in the Temple of Hathor at Dendera, Egypt, this monumental sandstone celestial map unites Greek, Babylonian, and Egyptian astronomy within a single stone disc of zodiac signs and star deities.
catalog-0024.look: Around the outer ring, twelve divine figures hold up the heavens, while inside spiral the familiar zodiac signs we still recognize today—Aries, Leo, Libra, and more. From the exact eclipses carved into the stone, astronomers were able to pinpoint this night sky to around 50 BC.

catalog-0025.title: Napoleon III Apartments
catalog-0025.author: Second Empire Decorative Artisans
catalog-0025.background: Completed in 1861 during the Second Empire of Napoleon III, these state reception rooms served the Minister of State. Stepping inside brings vividly to life the Louvre's centuries as a royal palace and a dazzling stage for 19th-century imperial politics.
catalog-0025.look: Look up and take in the opulent symphony of deep crimson velvet, gilded stucco, and monumental crystal chandeliers. Beyond the paintings on the walls, every surface showcases France's finest Second Empire cabinetmakers, weavers, and metalworkers united in a living total work of art.

catalog-0026.title: The Intervention of the Sabine Women
catalog-0026.author: Jacques-Louis David
catalog-0026.background: Conceived while David was imprisoned during the Reign of Terror and completed in 1799, this monumental canvas depicts the legendary clash between Romans and Sabines halted when women caught between both sides rush into the fray cradling their infants.
catalog-0026.look: Focus on Hersilia in the center, dressed in pure white with arms outstretched to hold the two warriors apart. After years of Revolutionary bloodshed, David embedded an urgent plea for reconciliation—imploring the French people to lay down their hatred.

catalog-0028.title: La Belle Jardinière
catalog-0028.author: Raphael
catalog-0028.background: Painted when Raphael was just twenty-four as a crowning achievement of his Florentine years, this work stands among his finest Madonna and Child compositions. In a serene pastoral setting, Mary, the infant Jesus, and young Saint John the Baptist are bound in effortless harmony.
catalog-0028.look: Observe the rock-solid pyramidal structure holding the three figures together, and notice the tender detail of Jesus resting his tiny foot atop Mary's. Blending compositional rigor learned from Leonardo with Raphael's own radiant warmth and clear blue skies, it radiates pure serenity.

catalog-0029.title: The Madonna of Chancellor Rolin
catalog-0029.author: Jan van Eyck
catalog-0029.background: Flemish master Jan van Eyck painted this jewel-like panel for Nicolas Rolin, powerful chancellor of the Duchy of Burgundy. Pushing oil painting to astonishing precision, he rendered microscopic details with an almost luminous sheen.
catalog-0029.look: Peer through the triple arches in the background at the arched bridge and miniature city bustling with tiny figures. Standing on the bridge, two small men gaze out over the river—and the one wearing a red turban is often thought to be a subtle self-portrait of Van Eyck himself.

catalog-0031.title: The Fortune Teller
catalog-0031.author: Caravaggio
catalog-0031.background: Painted when Caravaggio was in his mid-twenties, this sharp, playful genre scene captures a fleeting moment on a Roman street. A stylish young nobleman stops to have his palm read, unaware that he is the target of a clever sleight of hand.
catalog-0031.look: Watch their hands closely. While the young woman locks eyes with the youth and charms him into dropping his guard, her nimble fingers quietly slip the gold ring right off his finger. Caravaggio tells an entire psychological comedy through glances and touch alone.

catalog-0032.title: Et in Arcadia ego (The Arcadian Shepherds)
catalog-0032.author: Nicolas Poussin
catalog-0032.background: Nicolas Poussin, father of 17th-century French Classicism, meditates quietly on life and mortality through shepherds gathered in the idyllic land of Arcadia. The Latin inscription carved into the tomb—'Et in Arcadia ego' ('Even in Arcadia, there am I')—lingers with solemn resonance.
catalog-0032.look: Look at the kneeling shepherd tracing the engraved letters with his finger, and notice his own shadow falling directly beside them onto the stone. Even in paradise, death is ever present—a sober truth watched over silently by the stately, goddess-like woman standing on the right.

money.title: The Moneylender and His Wife
money.author: Quentin Metsys
money.background: Painted in 1514 in the bustling commercial port of Antwerp, Quentin Metsys's moralizing genre scene captures a couple caught between spiritual devotion and worldly wealth: the husband weighs gold coins while his wife turns the pages of an illuminated prayer book, unable to resist glancing at the gold.
money.look: Lean in and peer into the small convex mirror placed at the front center of the table. Inside its curved reflection, you can clearly make out a church spire outside the window and a customer in a red cap waiting at the door—a Northern Renaissance tour de force pulling the world beyond the frame right into the room.

catalog-0033.title: Gabrielle d'Estrées and One of Her Sisters
catalog-0033.author: School of Fontainebleau
catalog-0033.background: Created by an artist of the late 16th-century School of Fontainebleau, this remains one of art history's most enigmatic portraits. Seated in a draped bath, Gabrielle d'Estrées—beloved mistress of King Henry IV—shares a startling gesture with one of her sisters.
catalog-0033.look: Though her sister's gesture of pinching Gabrielle's nipple looks bizarre to modern eyes, it was a coded visual congratulation celebrating pregnancy and approaching motherhood. Every detail confirms the good news: the maid sewing baby garments in the background and the royal ring Gabrielle holds in her left hand.

marly.title: The Marly Horses
marly.author: Guillaume Coustou
marly.background: Commissioned for the grounds of Louis XV's Château de Marly and completed in 1745, Guillaume Coustou's dynamic pair of marble groups once flanked the entrance to the Champs-Élysées after the French Revolution before the originals were brought indoors here for preservation.
marly.look: Look up at the wild manes, flared nostrils, and taut muscles of the young grooms straining to rein in the rearing stallions. As natural daylight shifts through the courtyard's glass roof throughout the day, changing shadows make the horses seem ready to burst into motion.

catalog-0034.title: Frieze of Archers
catalog-0034.author: Ancient Persia
catalog-0034.background: Dating to around 510 BC, this monumental glazed-brick relief once adorned the palace walls of Persian King Darius I at Susa. Carrying spears and bows, the royal elite guards known as the Immortals march in stately procession.
catalog-0034.look: Marvel at the vivid turquoise blues and warm ochres that still glow after 2,500 years. Notice subtle variations in the soldiers' patterned robes and poised expressions—rhythmic repetition conveying both the discipline of a vast empire and extraordinary ceramic craftsmanship.

catalog-0036.title: Pyxis of al-Mughira
catalog-0036.author: Umayyad Artisans of Córdoba
catalog-0036.background: Carved from elephant ivory in 968, this cylindrical lidded box bears an inscription naming Ibrahim ibn al-Mughira. Its intricate botanical and animal motifs offer a vivid glimpse into the refined court culture of Umayyad Spain.
catalog-0036.look: Follow the bands of animals and foliage wrapping seamlessly around the curved surface. Notice how every millimeter of background space is balanced with delicate precision—an astonishing density of artistry packed into a small vessel.

catalog-0037.title: Statue of Ebih-Il
catalog-0037.author: Ancient Mesopotamia
catalog-0037.background: Dedicated around 2400 BC at the Temple of Ishtar in the Mesopotamian city-state of Mari, this remarkably preserved alabaster statue portrays the high official Ebih-Il, complete with inlaid eyes of deep blue lapis lazuli.
catalog-0037.look: Look at those clear blue eyes and serene smile, astonishingly vivid after forty-four centuries. With hands clasped calmly over his chest and a sculpted tufted fleece skirt, he stands in perpetual, reverent prayer before the goddess.

catalog-0038.title: Sarcophagus of the Spouses
catalog-0038.author: Ancient Etruscan Artisans
catalog-0038.background: Created around 520 BC by the mysterious Etruscan civilization of ancient Italy, this terracotta funerary monument reflects a culture that viewed death not as a grim ending, but as the joyful continuation of earthly banquets in the afterlife.
catalog-0038.look: Notice the husband draping his arm tenderly around his wife's shoulders as both share the same gentle smile atop their banquet couch. While Greek women of that era rarely dined alongside men at feasts, Etruscan spouses appear here as equals bound in lifelong affection.

catalog-0039.title: Monzón Lion
catalog-0039.author: Islamic Artisans
catalog-0039.background: Originating in the medieval Islamic world, this cast-bronze vessel takes the proud form of a lion. Fitted with an opening on its back, it is thought to have served as an aquamanile for pouring water—marrying fierce animal sculpture with everyday function.
catalog-0039.look: Examine the lion's expressive face and sturdy paws to see how its feline power is stylized. Trace the path from the hinged opening on its back to the spout at its mouth, and look closely at the finely engraved patterns and Arabic inscriptions embellishing its flanks.

catalog-0040.title: Saint Mary Magdalene
catalog-0040.author: Gregor Erhart
catalog-0040.background: Carved from a single trunk of limewood in the early 16th century by German sculptor Gregor Erhart, this life-size polychrome figure depicts Saint Mary Magdalene gazing upward in prayer, her body veiled only by cascading locks of golden hair.
catalog-0040.look: Originally, this sculpture hung from chains beneath a church vault, surrounded by four angels as though floating in midair. Walk around it to appreciate how its fluid contours hold together seamlessly from all 360 degrees, with strands of golden hair following every curve of her form.

catalog-0041.title: Winter
catalog-0041.author: Giuseppe Arcimboldo
catalog-0041.background: Part of a celebrated series personifying the Four Seasons, Arcimboldo built this human profile entirely out of gnarled branches, bark, and winter fruits—a witty fusion of Renaissance courtly amusement and keen observation of nature.
catalog-0041.look: Look first at the overall profile, then hunt for the individual plants that compose it: knotted tree bark turns into the weathered skin of an old man's face. Stepping back and moving closer continually transforms what you see.

catalog-0042.title: Spring
catalog-0042.author: Giuseppe Arcimboldo
catalog-0042.background: An allegory of spring composed entirely of blossoms and leaves, this portrait gathers the abundance of the season into a single figure—an ingenious visual puzzle that reveals two completely different images from afar and up close.
catalog-0042.look: Take in the smiling profile from a distance, then step closer to pick out each flower one by one. Watch how petals shift in color across the cheek and collar, and compare its lush botanical palette with the barren branches of Winter beside it.

catalog-0043.title: The Burial of Atala
catalog-0043.author: Anne-Louis Girodet
catalog-0043.background: Painted in 1808 by David's pupil Girodet, this early Romantic masterpiece illustrates the tragic finale of Chateaubriand's popular novel Atala: torn between a sacred vow of chastity and earthly love, the young heroine takes her own life and is laid to rest in a cave by her lover and an elderly priest.
catalog-0043.look: Moonlight streaming from the cave entrance bathes only Atala's pale face and folded hands in an ethereal glow. Notice the poignant contrast between Chactas, the young man collapsing in grief at her feet, and the aged Father Aubry bowed in quiet prayer.

catalog-0044.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx
catalog-0044.author: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
catalog-0044.background: Painted at twenty-eight while Ingres was studying in Rome and later expanded, this mythological masterpiece captures the tense confrontation between the young hero Oedipus and the monstrous Sphinx, whom he defeats with intellect and steady resolve alone.
catalog-0044.look: Peer into the rocky shadow beneath the Sphinx on the left—there lie the bleached bones of travelers who failed her riddle. Facing that grim warning without flinching, Oedipus meets the monster's gaze head-on in a profile of calm, heroic determination.

catalog-0045.title: Portrait of Madame Récamier
catalog-0045.author: Jacques-Louis David
catalog-0045.background: Painted in 1800, this unfinished portrait by Jacques-Louis David depicts twenty-three-year-old Juliette Récamier, celebrated as the paragon of wit and beauty in Parisian high society. Reclining barefoot on a daybed in an austere, ancient Roman-inspired interior, her refined simplicity set a defining fashion for the era.
catalog-0045.look: Notice the drastically pared-back background, her bare toes, and her poised glance back over her shoulder. David took so long working on the painting that Madame Récamier grew impatient and turned to another artist—leaving the background unfinished to this day.

catalog-0046.title: Madame Vigée-Lebrun and Her Daughter, Julie
catalog-0046.author: Élisabeth-Louise Vigée-Lebrun
catalog-0046.background: Painted in 1789—the very year the French Revolution erupted—by Marie-Antoinette's favorite court painter, this tender self-portrait captures the deep bond between mother and daughter. Note that according to the official Louvre database, it is currently not on display.
catalog-0046.look: Look at how mother and daughter press their cheeks together in an intimate embrace that forms a single sweeping triangle. While aristocratic portraiture of the time demanded stiff formal attire, Vigée-Lebrun chose simple, classical dress and natural smiles to convey maternal love directly.

catalog-0047.title: The Young Martyr
catalog-0047.author: Paul Delaroche
catalog-0047.background: Painted by nineteenth-century French artist Paul Delaroche amidst profound grief following the death of his beloved wife, this haunting religious work depicts a young Christian girl drowned in the Tiber for her faith in ancient Rome, floating upon the dark water beneath a miraculous halo.
catalog-0047.look: Observe the serene face of the maiden drifting across the nocturnal river and the faint, ethereal halo hovering above her head. Two shadowy figures watching from the distant bank deepen the unspoken sorrow and quiet reverence. The painting is currently on loan to the Louvre-Lens.

catalog-0048.title: The Apotheosis of Homer
catalog-0048.author: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
catalog-0048.background: Created in 1827 as a ceiling painting for the Louvre Palace, this monumental work serves as Ingres's grand manifesto of Neoclassicism. Centered on the ancient Greek poet Homer, it gathers forty-six of the greatest artists, poets, and philosophers from antiquity to modern times.
catalog-0048.look: The two women seated at Homer's feet are personifications of the Iliad and the Odyssey. Surrounding them are luminaries from Raphael, Dante, and Michelangelo to Shakespeare and Mozart—yet not a single Romantic rival, such as Delacroix, was permitted to appear.

catalog-0049.title: The Coronation of Marie de' Medici
catalog-0049.author: Peter Paul Rubens
catalog-0049.background: This resplendent canvas belongs to Baroque master Peter Paul Rubens's twenty-four-painting cycle celebrating the life of French Queen Marie de' Medici. It depicts the lavish ceremony of 1610 at the Basilica of Saint-Denis, where Marie was crowned Queen of France.
catalog-0049.look: Painted nearly two centuries before David's Coronation of Napoleon, this composition actually served as a direct model for it. At the center, the kneeling queen is showered with flowers and gold coins by mythological spirits above, transforming a historical state ceremony into grand Baroque theater.

catalog-0050.title: Spring (The Earthly Paradise)
catalog-0050.author: Nicolas Poussin
catalog-0050.background: Painted late in life as part of Nicolas Poussin's final masterpiece cycle, The Four Seasons, this work bathes the biblical Garden of Eden in the crisp light of a spring morning, capturing the tranquil perfection of Paradise before the Fall.
catalog-0050.look: Spot Eve in the center pointing toward the forbidden fruit tree, and look up to the upper left to find the small figure of the Creator floating among the clouds. Soft raking morning light illuminates the lush forest, preserving a fleeting moment of unspoiled stillness just before temptation and exile.

catalog-0051.title: Saint Sebastian
catalog-0051.author: Andrea Mantegna
catalog-0051.background: A masterwork by fifteenth-century Italian Renaissance visionary Andrea Mantegna, uniting dazzling perspective with an ardent passion for classical antiquity. Pierced by arrows yet gazing heavenward, the noble figure of Saint Sebastian stands beside ruined marble columns.
catalog-0051.look: Look closely at the white cloud drifting in the blue sky at the upper left—it subtly takes the shape of a rider on horseback. Meanwhile, the shattered fragments of ancient Roman sculpture lying at the saint's feet symbolize the triumph of the new Christian faith over the crumbling pagan world.

catalog-0052.title: An Old Man and His Grandson
catalog-0052.author: Domenico Ghirlandaio
catalog-0052.background: Created by fifteenth-century Florentine master Domenico Ghirlandaio, this deeply moving Renaissance portrait captures wordless affection between grandfather and grandson. By refusing to conceal the elder man's rhinophyma—a bulbous, disfigured nose—the artist makes his inner gentleness shine all the brighter.
catalog-0052.look: Watch how the young child looks up at his grandfather's swollen nose without a trace of fear, meeting him instead with pure trust and love. The quiet warmth passing between their eyes has touched visitors for more than five centuries.

catalog-0053.title: Portrait of a Man (Il Condottiere)
catalog-0053.author: Antonello da Messina
catalog-0053.background: Sicilian painter Antonello da Messina revolutionized portraiture here by fusing Northern Netherlandish oil glazing techniques with Italian sculptural form. Because of the sitter's piercing, formidable stare, the painting later earned the nickname Il Condottiere—'the mercenary captain.'
catalog-0053.look: Meet the man's razor-sharp, uncompromising gaze, which seems ready to step right out of the frame. The faint scar running from his left cheek to his lip and his tightly set mouth speak to a life hardened by the turbulent world of fifteenth-century Italy.

catalog-0054.title: The Pastoral Concert
catalog-0054.author: Attributed to Titian
catalog-0054.background: A poetic emblem of the Venetian Renaissance's golden age, believed to have been conceived by Giorgione and completed by the young Titian. Note that according to the official Louvre database, this work is currently not on display.
catalog-0054.look: Two clothed young men play the lute while two nude women beside them draw water from a spring and hold a flute. This dreamy allegory blends real musicians with the invisible Muses of poetry and music, sharing the same sunlit landscape.

catalog-0055.title: Man with a Glove
catalog-0055.author: Titian
catalog-0055.background: Painted by Venetian master Titian in his early thirties, this portrait epitomizes aristocratic poise. Holding one leather glove in his left hand while wearing the other on his right, the young nobleman exudes quiet intellect and understated melancholy.
catalog-0055.look: Notice how the pale face, the two hands, and a small triangle of white shirt emerge from the deep black garments and dark background. By restricting his palette to the barest essentials, Titian gives breathtaking prominence to the young man's thoughtful composure.

catalog-0056.title: The Virgin of the Rabbit
catalog-0056.author: Titian
catalog-0056.background: Rendered in the sumptuous, glowing color characteristic of Titian and the Venetian school, this intimate scene portrays the Holy Family with disarming tenderness. The Virgin Mary gently holds a white rabbit in her left hand while the Christ Child, cradled by Saint Catherine, reaches toward it with innocent delight.
catalog-0056.look: The white rabbit beneath Mary's hand is an ancient emblem of both purity and fertility, symbolizing the Virgin's innocence. From the twilight glow over the Dolomite peaks behind them to Joseph quietly watching at the far right, the entire scene radiates warmth and serenity.

catalog-0057.title: Statuette of a Blue Hippopotamus
catalog-0057.author: Ancient Egyptian artisan
catalog-0057.background: This small faience figure of a hippopotamus is coated in vibrant blue glaze. To the ancient Egyptians, the hippopotamus embodied both formidable strength and peril, and placing such figurines in tombs expressed a wish for rebirth.
catalog-0057.look: Search its rounded body for painted motifs of marsh plants. The bright blue glaze evokes the life-giving waters of the Nile, while the contrast between its stubby legs and plump torso gives the piece unmistakable charm.

catalog-0058.title: Chapel of the Tomb of Akhethotep
catalog-0058.author: Ancient Egyptian artisans
catalog-0058.background: This Old Kingdom funerary chapel was dismantled and reconstructed inside the Louvre. Its carved wall reliefs depict farming, daily labor, and offerings—inscribed to ensure the deceased would continue to enjoy sustenance in the afterlife.
catalog-0058.look: Observe what the figures along the walls are carrying and crafting, and look for where hieroglyphs align directly with the scenes. Walking inside the room itself lets you experience how a tomb chapel functioned as a sacred space.

catalog-0059.title: Statue of Karomama
catalog-0059.author: Ancient Egyptian metalworker
catalog-0059.background: This bronze statue portrays Karomama, a high-ranking priestess and Divine Adoratrice of the god Amun. It showcases the exquisite metalworking mastery of Egypt's Third Intermediate Period while reflecting the close ties between royalty and the priesthood.
catalog-0059.look: Follow the graceful contours of her pleated gown and trace the delicate inlaid decorative lines still visible on the surface. Though modest in scale, her upright stance commands quiet authority.

catalog-0060.title: Colossal Statue of Ramesses II
catalog-0060.author: Ancient Egyptian sculptor
catalog-0060.background: This monumental sculpture depicts Ramesses II, one of Egypt's longest-reigning and most celebrated pharaohs. By portraying the king on a colossal scale, the work projects absolute royal authority and the idealized image of ancient Egyptian kingship.
catalog-0060.look: Let your gaze travel from the base up to his face. The strictly symmetrical posture conveys unshakable stability and power, while the royal crown and carved cartouches proclaim the pharaoh's name.

catalog-0061.title: Relief of a Hero Holding a Lion (called Gilgamesh)
catalog-0061.author: Ancient Assyrian artisans
catalog-0061.background: Carved for an Assyrian royal palace wall, this towering relief depicts a giant clutching a lion in his arm. Often identified with the legendary hero Gilgamesh—though scholars still debate his exact identity—the monumental figure embodies royal might.
catalog-0061.look: Compare the scale of the hero's muscular arm with the lion held beneath it, and notice his rare frontal pose among surrounding figures shown in profile. Don't miss the crisp, intricate carving of his curled beard and hair.

catalog-0062.title: Stele of Baal with Thunderbolt
catalog-0062.author: Ancient Ugaritic artisan
catalog-0062.background: Excavated at Ugarit on the Syrian coast, this carved stone stele portrays the storm god Baal wielding a weapon symbolizing lightning. In an agricultural society, the deity who commanded life-giving rains held supreme importance.
catalog-0062.look: Look at the raised arm gripping his club and the stylized spear sprouting plant motifs down toward his feet. Set against the flat stone slab, the god's striding silhouette projects raw energy.

catalog-0063.title: Roll-Top Desk of Marie-Antoinette
catalog-0063.author: Jean-Henri Riesener
catalog-0063.background: Crafted for Queen Marie-Antoinette, this royal writing desk features a curved rolling lid designed to conceal papers and correspondence. It marries opulent materials with the pinnacle of eighteenth-century French cabinetmaking.
catalog-0063.look: Study the sweeping curve of the cylinder top and the balanced arrangement of the drawers. Enjoy the interplay between richly grained wood marquetry and gilt-bronze mounts—an everyday piece of furniture elevated into fine sculpture.

catalog-0064.title: Milo of Croton
catalog-0064.author: Pierre Puget
catalog-0064.background: Pierre Puget carved the tragic legend of the aging Greek wrestler Milo of Croton, whose hand became trapped in a split tree trunk, leaving him defenseless against a wild lion. As a cautionary tale against hubris in fading strength, it brims with fierce Baroque emotion.
catalog-0064.look: Trace the violent twist of his body starting from the trapped hand, and compare his agonized expression with the lunging beast. Walk around the sculpture to feel how the tension shifts from every angle.

catalog-0065.title: Fame Riding Pegasus
catalog-0065.author: Antoine Coysevox
catalog-0065.background: Commissioned for the royal gardens to glorify the Sun King, Louis XIV, this dynamic marble group shows the allegorical figure of Fame astride the winged horse Pegasus, poised to carry news of royal victories across the world.
catalog-0065.look: Follow the upward surge of the rearing horse and the sweeping gesture of Fame's arms, comparing the carved feathers of the wings with the flowing mane. Imagining the group mounted high on a pedestal amplifies its dramatic sense of flight.

catalog-0066.title: Cupid Carving His Bow from the Club of Hercules
catalog-0066.author: Edmé Bouchardon
catalog-0066.background: Here, the young god of love fashions a bow out of the mighty club of Hercules. A tour de force of delicate eighteenth-century French anatomical carving, the sculpture turns heroic mythological strength into a playful triumph of love.
catalog-0066.look: Look down at the massive club at his feet and then up to his nimble hands at work, noting the subtle musculature of the adolescent figure. Move around the pedestal to appreciate the graceful, spiraling composition.

catalog-0067.title: Flying Mercury
catalog-0067.author: Giambologna
catalog-0067.background: This bronze captures Mercury, messenger of the gods, at the exact instant he launches into the sky. Celebrated for the airy lightness of late Renaissance Mannerism, the entire figure appears effortlessly suspended on the tiniest point of contact.
catalog-0067.look: Follow the line upward from the single supporting foot—balanced on a puff of wind—to the limbs extending in opposing directions. Walking around the bronze reveals how its silhouette transforms with every step.

catalog-0068.title: Sleeping Hermaphroditus
catalog-0068.author: Ancient Roman sculptor
catalog-0068.background: This ancient Roman marble portrays the mythological figure of Hermaphroditus reclining in sleep; centuries later, Gian Lorenzo Bernini sculpted the sumptuous tufted mattress beneath. It is a work designed to surprise viewers as their perspective shifts.
catalog-0068.look: Start by viewing the figure from behind, where the graceful curve of the back looks wholly feminine, then walk around to the opposite side to discover the dual anatomy. Notice too the contrast between the ancient marble body and Bernini's Baroque mattress.

catalog-0069.title: Statue of Senusret III as an Old Man
catalog-0069.author: Ancient Egyptian sculptor
catalog-0069.background: Unlike idealized royal portraits, this Middle Kingdom sculpture depicts Pharaoh Senusret III with the weathered features of age. Rare signs of weariness and deep contemplation temper royal majesty with unmistakable individuality.
catalog-0069.look: Study the heavy creases beneath his eyes and the lines framing his mouth, contrasting the calm stability of his torso with the complexity of his face. Observe how his expression seems to change between a frontal and a three-quarter view.

catalog-0070.title: Bust of Akhenaten
catalog-0070.author: Ancient Egyptian sculptor
catalog-0070.background: Associated with Pharaoh Akhenaten, instigator of Egypt's radical religious revolution, this sculpture exemplifies the distinctive Amarna style. Its elongated, stylized features mark a striking departure from centuries of traditional royal portraiture.
catalog-0070.look: Notice the unusually long contours of the head and neck, alongside the full lips and heavy-lidded, softened eyes. Compare this expressive, unconventional styling with earlier royal statues nearby.

catalog-0071.title: Diana of Gabii
catalog-0071.author: Ancient Roman sculptor
catalog-0071.background: This Roman marble statue, derived from a classical Greek prototype, depicts the hunting goddess Diana fastening her cloak. It captures a fleeting, everyday gesture within a composition of serene, harmonious poise.
catalog-0071.look: Focus on her hands reaching up to clasp the brooch at her shoulder, and see how the cascading folds of drapery echo the twist of her body. Viewing the statue from the side reveals the subtle interplay of her raised arms.

catalog-0072.title: Baptistère de Saint Louis
catalog-0072.author: Mamluk metalworker
catalog-0072.background: Created in the fourteenth century in Mamluk Egypt or Syria, this large inlaid metal basin was later brought to France and used for royal baptisms—though it actually dates from after the reign of King Louis IX, for whom it is named.
catalog-0072.look: Search the exterior frieze for horsemen and lively hunting scenes rendered in fine silver and gold inlay. Then follow the intricate patterns as they continue seamlessly over the rim into the interior of the basin.

catalog-0073.title: Statue of Tutankhamun Protected by Amun
catalog-0073.author: Ancient Egyptian sculptor
catalog-0073.background: In this dyad sculpture, the supreme deity Amun stands directly behind the young Pharaoh Tutankhamun, enveloping him in protection. The composition visibly affirms that earthly kingship rests under divine guardianship.
catalog-0073.look: Notice the towering figure of the god rising behind the smaller king and see where their bodies overlap. Seen straight on, protector and ruler merge into a single unified silhouette.

catalog-0074.title: Stele of Cleopatra VII
catalog-0074.author: Ancient Egyptian artisan
catalog-0074.background: Inscribed with the name of Cleopatra VII, last queen of the Ptolemaic dynasty, this stele demonstrates how traditional Egyptian visual conventions endured down to the final years of pharaonic rule, linking a famous historical figure directly to ancient hieroglyphs.
catalog-0074.look: Look for the carved hieroglyphs bearing the queen's name, and observe the rounded arch at the top alongside the formal arrangement of figures—an image of Cleopatra far removed from later Greco-Roman portraits.

catalog-0075.title: Voltaire Seated
catalog-0075.author: Jean-Antoine Houdon
catalog-0075.background: Jean-Antoine Houdon portrays the Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire in old age, wrapped in a classical robe that still hints at his frail, living frame beneath. Rather than relying on youthful idealization, the portrait radiates sheer intellectual vitality.
catalog-0075.look: Take in the weathered wrinkles and that famous, knowing half-smile. Compare the relaxed weight of his seated body with the piercing alertness of his eyes—accented all the more by the light drapery clinging to his form.

catalog-0076.title: Apollo and Daphne
catalog-0076.author: Nicolas Coustou
catalog-0076.background: Carved for royal garden display, this dramatic sculpture captures the mythological pursuit of the nymph Daphne by the god Apollo, freezing in marble the very moment her body begins to transform.
catalog-0076.look: Observe the charged space separating the two figures and the outstretched limbs that convey breathless pursuit. Look closely along Daphne's form for the emerging signs of bark and laurel leaves.

catalog-0077.title: The Bolt
catalog-0077.author: Jean-Honoré Fragonard
catalog-0077.background: Painted by eighteenth-century Rococo master Jean-Honoré Fragonard, this charged composition captures sudden romantic passion amid dramatic chiaroscuro. A young man stretches to slide the bolt shut on the bedroom door while a woman tries to hold him back in a breathless instant.
catalog-0077.look: Follow the bold diagonal formed by their bodies pointing straight toward the small brass bolt at the upper right, then notice the rumpled red bed on the left and the apple resting on the table—a classic biblical symbol of temptation. Rococo elegance meets Baroque theatricality here.

catalog-0078.title: The Ray
catalog-0078.author: Jean-Siméon Chardin
catalog-0078.background: Painted in 1728, this revolutionary still life propelled the unknown twenty-eight-year-old Jean-Siméon Chardin directly into the Royal Academy. Hanging a gutted skate on a kitchen wall beside a bristling black cat poised over oysters, Chardin renders every texture with astonishing immediacy.
catalog-0078.look: Contrast the translucent, raw flesh of the sliced ray with the arched spine and hissing fury of the cat. Later masters like Matisse and Cézanne studied this canvas tirelessly, learning that light and texture matter far more than lofty subjects.

catalog-0079.title: The Penitent Magdalene
catalog-0079.author: Georges de La Tour
catalog-0079.background: In this masterwork by seventeenth-century 'painter of the night' Georges de La Tour, a single candle illuminates a moment of profound quiet introspection. Having renounced worldly vanity, Mary Magdalene rests her hand on a skull, meditating on the fleeting nature of life.
catalog-0079.look: As nearly the entire room sinks into velvety darkness, the steady flame lights only Magdalene's chin, her fingertips, and the skull resting in her lap. Shed of jewels and framed by an unwavering candle, her stillness brings quiet clarity to the viewer as well.

catalog-0080.title: Diana Leaving the Bath
catalog-0080.author: François Boucher
catalog-0080.background: A signature work by François Boucher, darling of King Louis XV and Madame de Pompadour, this painting embodies the sweet, radiant refinement of the eighteenth-century Rococo court. The hunting goddess Diana relaxes effortlessly beside a woodland spring with her nymph attendant.
catalog-0080.look: Spot the tiny crescent moon gleaming on Diana's brow, identifying her as goddess of the moon. From the fallen rabbits and game birds at her feet to the blush-pink and powder-blue silks and pearlescent skin, Rococo splendor shines in every detail.

catalog-0081.title: Bathsheba at Her Bath
catalog-0081.author: Rembrandt van Rijn
catalog-0081.background: Painted by Rembrandt at forty-eight, at the height of his maturity, this work offers one of the deepest psychological portraits in Western art. Having just received King David's forbidden summons, Bathsheba sits suspended in quiet anguish between duty, desire, and guilt.
catalog-0081.look: Notice the letter gripped in Bathsheba's right hand and her distant, sorrowful gaze. Modeled on Hendrickje Stoffels, Rembrandt's devoted partner in his later years, she appears not as an idealized goddess, but as a real woman of weight, vulnerability, and quiet dignity.

catalog-0082.title: Self-Portrait at the Easel
catalog-0082.author: Rembrandt van Rijn
catalog-0082.background: Among the dozens of self-portraits Rembrandt painted across his lifetime, this deeply moving canvas was created at age fifty-four, after bankruptcy and bereavement had stripped away his fortune. Holding his palette, brushes, and maulstick, the aging artist faces us with unflinching honesty.
catalog-0082.look: Look at the deeply furrowed brow, sagging cheeks, and graying beard—yet behind those eyes burns an undimmed pride in his craft. The thick, rugged impasto of his brushwork feels like the very rings of a weathered tree.

catalog-0083.title: The Pilgrims at Emmaus
catalog-0083.author: Rembrandt van Rijn
catalog-0083.background: Painted in 1648, this hushed and deeply moving religious work captures the miracle at Emmaus: as the resurrected Christ breaks bread at a humble inn, two disciples suddenly recognize the Master they thought lost to the cross.
catalog-0083.look: Soft, radiant light glows gently behind Christ as he breaks the bread at center. Notice the contrast in reactions: the disciple on the right folds his hands in awe and the one on the left leans forward in astonishment, while the young servant carrying a dish remains completely oblivious to the miracle.

catalog-0084.title: Portrait of Mademoiselle Caroline Rivière
catalog-0084.author: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
catalog-0084.background: Painted when Ingres was just twenty-six, this unforgettable portrait captures Caroline Rivière, the fifteen-year-old daughter of a wealthy Parisian official. Tragically, the young girl died of illness only a few months after the canvas was completed.
catalog-0084.look: Admire her long white gloves, the soft swan's-down boa draped across her shoulders, and her clear, slightly hesitant gaze. Set against a crisp early spring landscape, the painting preserves the fragile beauty of fifteen forever.

catalog-0085.title: The Disembarkation of Marie de' Medici at Marseilles
catalog-0085.author: Peter Paul Rubens
catalog-0085.background: Part of the grand cycle glorifying Queen Marie de' Medici, this painting turns her arrival in France into a mythic triumph, seamlessly mingling historical pageantry with the deities of the sea.
catalog-0085.look: Watch the queen stepping down the gangplank from her ship while powerful sea gods and Nereids buoy the vessel below—uniting earthly history above with allegorical spectacle beneath.

catalog-0086.title: The Education of Marie de' Medici
catalog-0086.author: Peter Paul Rubens
catalog-0086.background: This canvas from the Medici cycle presents the queen's youth through classical allegory, depicting ancient gods bestowing wisdom, grace, and artistic gifts to elevate her real biography into timeless legend.
catalog-0086.look: Find the young princess at the center and see what each surrounding deity offers her, while swirling clouds and billowing drapery fill the scene with Baroque vitality.

catalog-0087.title: The Adoration of the Shepherds
catalog-0087.author: Georges de La Tour
catalog-0087.background: Painted late in Georges de La Tour's career, this Nativity scene bathes the newborn Christ in warm, intimate candlelight. By shielding the flame with his hand, Saint Joseph directs a gentle pool of light onto the infant Jesus alone.
catalog-0087.look: Watch how Joseph raises the candle at the right and cups his left hand to soften the glare—his fingers glowing translucent red against the flame. The tender smiles of the humble onlookers and the little lamb peeking up from below fill the night with quiet warmth.

catalog-0088.title: Portrait of Francis I
catalog-0088.author: Titian
catalog-0088.background: This crisp profile portrait of King Francis I of France was painted by Titian not from life, but from existing medallions and likenesses. Even so, it distills the commanding majesty of a Renaissance monarch with remarkable economy.
catalog-0088.look: Follow the sharp contour of his face and prominent nose, and take in the opulent velvet garments and plumed cap that signal royal status—creating a more formal distance than a full-face portrait.

catalog-0089.title: Head from Keros
catalog-0089.author: Cycladic sculptor
catalog-0089.background: Carved from marble in the Aegean Cyclades islands, this monumental head omits carved eyes or mouth, reducing the human face to a clean oval and a projecting nose. Its bold simplicity looks strikingly modern, though its original ritual purpose remains uncertain.
catalog-0089.look: Step to the side to see how sharply the nose rises from the flat plane of the face, and check whether the contours are perfectly symmetrical—marveling at how so few lines instantly read as human.

catalog-0090.title: The Coronation of the Virgin
catalog-0090.author: Fra Angelico
catalog-0090.background: In this radiant fifteenth-century altarpiece, Fra Angelico portrays the Virgin Mary receiving her heavenly crown surrounded by a host of angels and saints, expressing spiritual joy through harmonious symmetry and jewel-like color.
catalog-0090.look: Let your eyes expand outward from the central coronation to compare the robes and expressions of each angel and saint one by one. Even with such a dense gathering, the balanced left-and-right arrangement creates serene heavenly order.

catalog-0091.title: Self-Portrait with a Thistle
catalog-0091.author: Albrecht Dürer
catalog-0091.background: Painted when the German master Albrecht Dürer was just twenty-two, this landmark work helped establish the self-portrait as an independent art form. Scholars still debate whether the thistle in his hand alludes to betrothal, fidelity, or Christ's Passion.
catalog-0091.look: Compare the sprig of sea holly in his fingers with the steady, searching expression in his eyes. Notice the meticulous rendering of every curl of hair and fold of fabric, revealing how the young artist chose to present himself to the world.

catalog-0092.title: Woman with a Mirror
catalog-0092.author: Titian
catalog-0092.background: In this lush Venetian painting, a young woman arranges her hair before a mirror held by a man in the shadows behind her—turning the very acts of looking and being looked at into the painting's theme through rich layers of color and texture.
catalog-0092.look: Check what each of the two mirrors actually reflects, and compare the varied textures of her cascading hair, luminous skin, and silk sleeves. Expanding your gaze to include the man holding the mirror subtly shifts the entire relationship of the scene.

catalog-0093.title: The Antaios Krater
catalog-0093.author: Euphronios
catalog-0093.background: This grand ancient Greek wine-mixing vessel depicts the wrestling match between Herakles and the giant Antaios. Using the red-figure technique—leaving the figures in warm clay red against a glossy black background—Euphronios turns the curved vase into a vivid stage for myth.
catalog-0093.look: Trace where the wrestlers' locked arms and legs intertwine, and look closely for the delicate black lines defining taut muscles and hair against the dark glaze. Because the scene wraps around the vessel, be sure to view it from multiple angles.

catalog-0094.title: Lion Crushing a Serpent
catalog-0094.author: Antoine-Louis Barye
catalog-0094.background: Nineteenth-century sculptor Antoine-Louis Barye captures a fierce struggle between a lion and a serpent. Rejecting decorative idealization, he studied live animal anatomy to infuse every tensed muscle and pose with raw, untamed vitality on a compact scale.
catalog-0094.look: Focus on the clash between the lion's massive forepaw and the coiling serpent, and read the animal's furrowed brow and arched back to anticipate its next strike. Moving around the bronze reveals shifting lines of force in the combat.

catalog-0095.title: Full-Length Portrait of the Marquise de Pompadour
catalog-0095.author: Maurice-Quentin de La Tour
catalog-0095.background: This portrait depicts the Marquise de Pompadour, who wielded immense influence at the court of King Louis XV. Surrounding her are books and musical scores that attest to her refined cultural education. Together, these elements convey both her glittering attire and her intellect.
catalog-0095.look: Look beyond her sumptuous gown to spot the books and sheet music resting on the table. Notice how her facial expression and the poise of her hands radiate calm self-assurance. Step closer to appreciate the soft, layered hues unique to pastel.

catalog-0096.title: Ivory Plaque Depicting the Triumph of an Emperor
catalog-0096.author: Byzantine Artisan
catalog-0096.background: This sixth-century ivory relief celebrates the triumph of an emperor, shown on horseback at the center as surrounding figures pay him homage. While some scholars identify the ruler as Emperor Justinian, his identity cannot be confirmed with certainty.
catalog-0096.look: Begin with the central equestrian figure of the emperor, then shift your gaze to the smaller scenes above and below to see who gathers to celebrate his victory. Notice the remarkable sense of depth carved into such a thin sheet of ivory.

catalog-0097.title: David and Goliath
catalog-0097.author: Daniele da Volterra
catalog-0097.background: This double-sided painting portrays the Old Testament duel from two distinct vantage points. Created during a period of lively debate over whether painting or sculpture was the superior art, it reveals a different moment of the dramatic clash depending on which side you view.
catalog-0097.look: Walk around to view both the front and the back in turn, comparing the twist of the bodies and the position of the sword. Together, these two opposing perspectives unite to complete a single fluid motion.

catalog-0098.title: The Abduction of Helen
catalog-0098.author: Guido Reni
catalog-0098.background: This canvas depicts the mythological episode that sparked the Trojan War. Arranged with measured classical balance, the composition conveys a momentous upheaval through surprisingly restrained expressions.
catalog-0098.look: Compare Helen at the center with the figures clustered around her, and follow how their hand gestures guide the direction of the story. Notice the striking contrast between the soft palette and the high drama of the subject.

catalog-0099.title: The Supper at Emmaus
catalog-0099.author: Paolo Veronese
catalog-0099.background: Here, the resurrected Christ reveals himself to his disciples in a scene transposed into the setting of a lavish Venetian banquet. Everyday dining and sacred miracle unfold side by side.
catalog-0099.look: Locate Christ at the center and study the varied reactions of those seated around him. Take in the delicate colors of the tableware and garments, and compare this scene with Veronese's monumental Wedding at Cana.

catalog-0100.title: Portrait of a Venetian Woman (La Belle Nani)
catalog-0100.author: Paolo Veronese
catalog-0100.background: This portrait captures a woman dressed in opulent attire, though the sitter's exact identity remains uncertain. Her rich jewelry and fine fabrics offer a vivid glimpse into Venetian high society of the era.
catalog-0100.look: Focus on the composed serenity of her face before picking out the ornaments gleaming against her dark gown. Notice how the graceful placement of her hands underscores her poise and nobility.

catalog-0101.title: Jupiter Hurling Thunderbolts at the Vices
catalog-0101.author: Paolo Veronese
catalog-0101.background: This allegorical painting shows the god Jupiter driving away the Vices. Originally designed to be viewed from below in an elevated setting, it uses classical mythology to proclaim authority and moral order.
catalog-0101.look: Trace a line from the god's thunderbolt-wielding hand down to the tumbling figures beneath him. Observe the sharp opposition between upward reach and headlong fall, heightened by the contrast between the bright sky and the shadowed lower zone.

catalog-0102.title: Paradise (The Coronation of the Virgin)
catalog-0102.author: Tintoretto
catalog-0102.background: A vast celestial host gathers in this religious composition, anchored by the Coronation of the Virgin at its heart. Its sweeping, energetic movement exemplifies the vitality of Venetian painting.
catalog-0102.look: Let your eye expand outward from the radiant center and observe which way the smaller figures are turned. Look closely to discover a circular current organizing this dense multitude.

catalog-0103.title: The Crucifixion
catalog-0103.author: Paolo Veronese
catalog-0103.background: Veronese depicts the Crucifixion of Christ surrounded by mourning witnesses. Even in a scene of profound sorrow, richly colored garments appear throughout, blending sacred narrative with Venetian decorative splendor.
catalog-0103.look: Observe the spacing of the figures around the cross and how their gazes and hand gestures express grief. Notice also how the hues of the sky shift the emotional tone of the entire scene.

catalog-0104.title: Portrait of Empress Joséphine
catalog-0104.author: Pierre-Paul Prud'hon
catalog-0104.background: Napoleon's empress is portrayed here resting amid a tranquil natural setting. Favoring intimate emotion over the imposing grandeur of an official state portrait, the work reveals the expressive range of early nineteenth-century portraiture.
catalog-0104.look: Take in her seated posture against the backdrop of surrounding trees. Notice how her luminous white dress stands out against the deep greens, and linger on her quiet, contemplative gaze.

catalog-0105.title: The Deluge
catalog-0105.author: Anne-Louis Girodet
catalog-0105.background: Inspired by the biblical Flood, this history painting captures a single dramatic instant as a family struggles to escape the rising waters. Its true subject is human vulnerability pushed to the brink.
catalog-0105.look: Look at the straining tree trunk ready to snap and the clinging bodies of the family members. Follow the chain of clasping hands, and notice how the dark, stormy backdrop intensifies their desperate peril.

catalog-0106.title: The Ghosts of Francesca and Paolo
catalog-0106.author: Ary Scheffer
catalog-0106.background: Drawn from Dante's Divine Comedy, this painting portrays the tragic lovers swept along by the winds of Hell while Dante and Virgil watch from the shadows. Scheffer transforms a literary episode into a deeply sentimental vision.
catalog-0106.look: Follow the sweeping motion of the embracing pair, then gauge the distance separating them from the two onlookers on the left. Notice how their pale skin emerging from the gloom heightens their spectral presence.

catalog-0107.title: The Nymph of Fontainebleau
catalog-0107.author: Benvenuto Cellini
catalog-0107.background: Conceived as a grand architectural ornament for a French royal palace, this monumental relief depicts a reclining water nymph. It stands as a testament to the Italian sculptors who brought Renaissance brilliance to the French court.
catalog-0107.look: See how the nymph's elongated pose adapts gracefully to the wide horizontal frame. Search around her body for the animals and emblems of water, and imagine the relief set high above a palace doorway.

catalog-0108.title: Mercury Carrying Off Psyche
catalog-0108.author: Adriaen de Vries
catalog-0108.background: This sculpture captures the mythological moment when Mercury, messenger of the gods, bears Psyche skyward after the lovers' reunion. The soaring upward posture creates an effortless sense of airborne motion.
catalog-0108.look: Let your eye travel from the base up to the raised arms of both figures, and notice how subtly the composition balances its weight. You can also connect this chapter of the myth with Canova's sculptures of Psyche nearby.

catalog-0109.title: Psyche and Cupid
catalog-0109.author: Antonio Canova
catalog-0109.background: In another sculptural interpretation of the same mythological lovers, Canova sought ideal perfection in youthful form. Quiet and tender, the work invites you to imagine the moments just before and after their embrace.
catalog-0109.look: Look for the delicate points where the two figures touch, and compare the soft carving of the wings with the flowing locks of hair. Walking slowly around the sculpture reveals shifting nuances of intimacy.

catalog-0110.title: Time Revealing Truth
catalog-0110.author: Giacomo Antonio Ponsonelli
catalog-0110.background: This allegorical group personifies abstract concepts—Time and Truth—through dynamic human figures. Its sweeping, theatrical energy is a hallmark of Baroque sculpture.
catalog-0110.look: Follow the exchange of gazes between the two figures and watch the dramatic motion of the drapery being drawn back. Ask yourself which figure embodies Time and which represents Truth.

catalog-0111.title: Nymph with a Scorpion
catalog-0111.author: Lorenzo Bartolini
catalog-0111.background: This nineteenth-century Neoclassical sculpture depicts a nymph startled by a scorpion. Bartolini turns a fleeting, everyday mishap into an exercise in graceful human proportion.
catalog-0111.look: Spot the tiny scorpion near her foot, then see how her sudden surprise registers in her expression and the positioning of her hands. Viewing the work from the side reveals the supple twist of her torso.

catalog-0112.title: Bust of Maria Duglioli Barberini
catalog-0112.author: Giuliano Finelli
catalog-0112.background: This seventeenth-century marble portrait bust captures its subject with extraordinary attention to the neckline and intricate attire. The serene composure of her face balances the sumptuous richness of the ornament.
catalog-0112.look: Examine the delicate carving of her hair and lace collar, comparing the smooth polish of her face with the deep shadows folded into her drapery. Be sure to admire the bust in profile as well.

catalog-0113.title: Hercules and the Hydra
catalog-0113.author: Italian Sculptor
catalog-0113.background: This mythological sculpture pits the hero Hercules against the many-headed Hydra. Centered on a raw clash of strength between man and monster, the tightly intertwined forms make the work captivating in the round.
catalog-0113.look: Follow the action from the hero's straining arms along the coiling necks of the beast, noting how a new silhouette emerges from every angle. Pay attention too to how the composition supports the hero's weight.

catalog-0114.title: The Wrestlers
catalog-0114.author: Philippe Magnier
catalog-0114.background: Showing two athletes locked in a fierce grapple, this work brings intense physical power to a classical garden subject. As you move around it, the overlapping bodies constantly reshape the composition.
catalog-0114.look: Trace each of the four arms and legs in turn and try to pinpoint where the group's center of gravity lies. Notice how the two bodies brace against and counterbalance one another.

catalog-0115.title: Hercules Fighting Achelous Transformed into a Serpent
catalog-0115.author: François-Joseph Bosio
catalog-0115.background: This sculpture dramatizes the legendary duel between Hercules and the river god Achelous, catching the exact instant the hero pins down his foe in serpent form. Its surging mythological energy was ideally suited to grand garden settings.
catalog-0115.look: Trace the coiling body of the serpent right up to Hercules's grip, and locate the muscles where his strength concentrates. Viewing the statue from a low angle makes the hero's figure appear even more imposing.

catalog-0116.title: Spartacus
catalog-0116.author: Denis Foyatier
catalog-0116.background: Sculpted in 1830, this figure represents the leader of the great slave rebellion in ancient Rome. Breaking free from his chains, he embodies an unyielding will for liberty, resonating strongly with the historical and political currents of the nineteenth century.
catalog-0116.look: Let your gaze rise from the broken chains at his feet up to the tension in his arm and the resolve on his face. Notice how his stance captures the split second just before he springs forward.

catalog-0117.title: Mercury Fastening His Sandal
catalog-0117.author: Jean-Baptiste Pigalle
catalog-0117.background: Here, the messenger of the gods pauses to adjust his winged footwear before taking flight. By catching the swift deity in a quiet moment of preparation, Pigalle transforms an everyday gesture into timeless myth.
catalog-0117.look: Look closely at the alignment of his hands and feet, and admire the effortless balance of his forward-leaning pose. You can almost sense the burst of motion about to follow.

catalog-0118.title: The Soldier of Marathon Announcing Victory
catalog-0118.author: Jean-Pierre Cortot
catalog-0118.background: This sculpture portrays the legendary Greek messenger delivering news of victory at Marathon. Cortot fuses the momentum of the runner's sprint with his utter exhaustion, distilling a heroic historic triumph into a single human body.
catalog-0118.look: Follow the outstretched reach of his arm and sense the forward rush in the tilt of his torso and legs. Then look at his face to see the profound weariness etched into his features.

catalog-0119.title: Sleeping Faun
catalog-0119.author: Edme Bouchardon
catalog-0119.background: Bouchardon depicts a mythological faun completely surrendered to sleep. In the relaxed, unforced anatomy, the sculptor's keen observation of nature shines through, evoking the peaceful stillness of a shaded garden.
catalog-0119.look: Observe how completely tension has drained from his face and hands, and check where the body rests its weight. Parts of the marble look remarkably soft to the touch.

catalog-0120.title: Perseus Freeing Andromeda
catalog-0120.author: Pierre Puget
catalog-0120.background: Commissioned for the gardens of Versailles, this group depicts the hero Perseus rescuing Andromeda from sacrifice to a sea monster. The taut, twisting movement of the figures exemplifies the expressive drama of the Baroque.
catalog-0120.look: Follow the direction of the figures' gazes and arms to feel the powerful forward surge carved directly into the stone. Notice how the overlap of their forms shifts with every step you take around it.

catalog-0121.title: Four Captives
catalog-0121.author: Martin Desjardins
catalog-0121.background: Originally crafted to adorn a royal monument in a Parisian square, these four figures personify vanquished nations in tribute to the king. Despite their royalist origins, these politically charged sculptures were preserved after the French Revolution.
catalog-0121.look: Compare the postures and facial expressions of all four captives, and look closely at the chains and decorative trophies at their feet. Try to picture them arranged around the base of the royal statue they once supported.

catalog-0122.title: Head of the Aphrodite of Knidos Type
catalog-0122.author: Ancient Roman Sculptor
catalog-0122.background: This marble head reproduces one of the most celebrated goddess statues of ancient Greece, a model copied repeatedly in later centuries. It illustrates how ideals of classical beauty were preserved and passed down across the ancient world.
